item.title: Tupelo man charged with felony shoplifting - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
TUPELO – A Tupelo man was arrested after police said he tried to leave a store without paying for several items.

According to the Tupelo Police Department, officers contacted employees at Scruggs, located at 3575 Tom Watson Drive, on May 11 in reference to shoplifting. Store personnel told officers an individual attempted to leave the store without paying for multiple items.

After further investigation, police arrested 22-year-old Erion M. Bass, of Tupelo, on May 15. Bass was charged with one count of felony shoplifting.

On May 17, Tupelo Municipal Court Judge Allen ordered Bass held on a $5,000 bond.

The case will be presented to the Lee County grand jury.

item.title: State inmate dies after being found unresponsive at George County facility - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
GEORGE COUNTY – A state inmate died Sunday morning after being found unresponsive at the George County Regional Correctional Facility.

According to the George County Sheriff’s Office, correctional facility staff reported the inmate was found unresponsive at approximately 7:55 a.m. Life-saving measures began in less than one minute, and responding personnel immediately administered CPR.

Officials said a pulse was regained before emergency medical services arrived.

The inmate, identified as 69-year-old Robert O. Pugh, was taken by ambulance to George County Hospital, where he was later pronounced dead at 8:03 a.m.

An autopsy will be conducted to determine the exact cause of death. Officials said there were no immediate findings to indicate anything other than natural causes at this time.

Sheriff Mitchell Mixon and the George County Sheriff’s Office extended condolences to Pugh’s family and loved ones.

item.title: Starkville man charged after hidden recording device found in home - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
STARKVILLE — A Starkville man was arrested Monday after police said a covert recording device was discovered inside a residence on Woodlawn Road.

Officers with the Starkville Police Department responded Sunday, May 17, to a report of a recording device that had allegedly been secretly placed inside the home.

Police said the suspect was not at the residence when officers initially arrived.

Following an investigation, officers arrested Scott Gronewold, 50, at about 11:49 p.m. Monday at his residence on Woodlawn Road.

Gronewold was charged with photographing or filming another person without permission where there is an expectation of privacy under Mississippi law.

According to police, the department’s tactical team assisted with the arrest after a threat assessment was conducted beforehand.

Authorities said Gronewold was transported to Baptist Memorial Hospital – Oktibbeha for medical and mental health treatment.

Anyone with information about the case or other criminal activity is asked to contact the Starkville Police Department at 662-323-4131, Golden Triangle Crime Stoppers at 800-530-7151, or submit an anonymous tip through the department’s website. Crime Stoppers may offer a cash reward for information.

item.title: Repeat felon convicted after being found with large Bowie knife in DeSoto County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
HERNANDO – A repeat convicted felon was sentenced to 10 years in prison after being convicted of possessing a weapon as a convicted felon, according to the DeSoto County District Attorney’s Office.

Prosecutors said Robert Long had been released from prison seven days before law enforcement found him in possession of a large Bowie knife. Because of his felony history, Long was prohibited from possessing any weapon.

The case went to trial, and a jury returned a guilty verdict after a one-day proceeding.

According to prosecutors, Long’s criminal history spans decades. Before 2024, he had been arrested 21 times in DeSoto County dating back to 2002 on various charges, including disturbance of the family and public drunk offenses. His record also includes multiple felony convictions, including felony fleeing.

Before the sentence was handed down, prosecutors said Long repeatedly used profanity and explicit language during the sentencing hearing.

District Attorney Matthew Barton said the case reflects his office’s continued focus on prosecuting habitual offenders and keeping repeat offenders off the streets before more serious violence occurs.

The case was investigated by the DeSoto County Sheriff’s Department and prosecuted by Assistant District Attorney Chase Morgan.

item.title: Reeves requests major disaster declaration for Mississippi counties hit by severe storms - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Gov. Tate Reeves has requested a major disaster declaration from President Donald Trump for five Mississippi counties impacted by severe storms earlier this month.

The request covers damage from severe storms, strong tornadoes, straight-line winds, hail and flash flooding that happened May 6-7. According to the governor’s office, the storms produced seven tornadoes, injured 26 people and damaged 425 homes across the state.

“Today, I requested a Major Disaster Declaration from President Trump,” Reeves said. “The state of Mississippi will continue to do everything in its power to help Mississippians rebuild and recover.”

The state is requesting individual assistance for Franklin, Lamar, Lawrence, Lincoln and Wilkinson counties.

FEMA-validated numbers show that in those five counties, 88 homes were destroyed, 112 homes received major damage, 140 had minor damage and 85 homes were affected.

The same five counties are also included in the request for public assistance. Joint damage assessments were conducted by FEMA and the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency, and officials said damage assessments indicate the threshold requirements have been met for public assistance.

According to the governor’s office, the request may be amended in the future to add additional counties if more damage is discovered and reported.

Individual assistance can include grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs to help people recover from the disaster.

Public assistance helps local governments and certain nonprofits recover from major disasters by providing grant assistance for debris removal, emergency protective measures and the restoration of public infrastructure.

The request must be approved by the president before federal assistance becomes available to local and county governments and certain nonprofits.

item.title: Mississippi Public Safety Summit begins tonight with keynote speaker Travis Howze - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
FLOWOOD — More than 600 law enforcement officers, firefighters, prosecutors and first responders from across the state are expected to gather this week for the 4th Annual Mississippi Public Safety Summit, which begins tonight in Flowood with keynote speaker Travis Howze.

The summit will be held May 19-22 at Sheraton Flowood The Refuge Hotel & Conference Center and is hosted by the Office of the Attorney General and the Mississippi Department of Public Safety.

Organizers said the event has grown steadily since its launch in 2023, when about 300 public safety professionals attended the inaugural summit. Attendance has since doubled, drawing workers from agencies and departments across Mississippi.

Tonight’s featured speaker, Howze, is a former U.S. Marine, police officer and firefighter who now travels internationally speaking about mental wellness, resiliency and trauma recovery for first responders and their families.

Howze is the creator of “Post Traumatic Purpose,” a program focused on leadership, mental health awareness and coping with trauma in emergency services professions. According to his biography, he developed the program after struggling with post-traumatic stress tied to traumatic experiences during his military and emergency services career, including surviving a 2007 warehouse fire in Charleston, South Carolina, that killed nine firefighters.

His presentation is expected to focus on the mental health challenges facing first responders, the importance of transparency and resiliency, and available resources for emergency personnel and their families.

The summit will also feature panel discussions, training sessions, the Governor’s First Responders Awards and a golf tournament during the four-day event.

item.title: MDWFP reminds boaters of education requirement during National Safe Boating Week - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks is reminding boaters about the state’s boater education requirement during National Safe Boating Week.

According to MDWFP, anyone born after June 30, 1980, must complete a boater education course before operating a motorized vessel on Mississippi’s public waters.

MDWFP offers both in-person and online boater education courses designed to help boaters understand navigation rules, recognize potential hazards and practice safe boating.

Those who need to complete the course can visit mdwfp.com/enforcement-education/boater-education.

MDWFP said it will share more safe boating tips throughout the week.

item.title: Man found fatally stabbed in Lee County, investigation ongoing - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
LEE COUNTY — A man died Saturday evening after authorities say he was found suffering from apparent stab wounds in the Pratts/Friendship community.

Deputies responded around 6:03 p.m. May 16 to County Road 1303 after receiving reports of an altercation involving an injured man, according to investigators.

When deputies arrived, they found Randy Hallmark unresponsive on the side of the road. Emergency medical personnel were already at the scene providing aid, but Hallmark later died from his injuries.

During the preliminary investigation, deputies also responded to a nearby residence where authorities believe the altercation began.

Investigators said one person of interest and one witness were taken into custody for investigative purposes.

Authorities said the case remains under active investigation. Once the investigation is complete, evidence and information gathered in the case will be presented to the district attorney’s office and then to the next available grand jury for review.

item.title: John Kyle State Park to reopen Friday after ice storm damage - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks announced that John W. Kyle State Park will reopen Friday, May 22, following months of cleanup from January’s damaging ice storm.

Officials said park reservations are now open for the Sardis park.

Several other state park facilities remain temporarily closed, including Wall Doxey State Park, George P. Cossar State Park and Tippah County Lake.

According to MDWFP, the closures remain necessary because of ongoing cleanup efforts involving storm debris, fallen trees and other hazards left behind by the January ice storm.

Officials said crews continue working to restore safe access for visitors and staff at the affected locations.

The department said park conditions are being assessed daily and additional updates on closures or reopening dates will be announced as they become available.

For updates on Mississippi State Parks, visit MDWFP State Parks or follow Mississippi State Parks on Facebook and Mississippi State Parks on Instagram .

item.title: Former police officer sentenced in child exploitation case - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Former Reservoir Police Officer Rodney Jernigan of Raleigh has been sentenced to 20 years to serve day-for-day in prison after pleading guilty to two counts of child exploitation, according to officials.

District Attorney Chris Hennis and Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced the sentencing, saying investigators and prosecutors remain committed to protecting children and holding offenders accountable.

“Our investigators and prosecutors are committed to holding individuals who exploit children accountable for their crimes,” Fitch said in a statement. “We are proud to work with our law enforcement partners to help these victims achieve justice and closure, and help protect other children from abuse.”

On May 15, 13th Circuit Court Judge Stanley Sorey sentenced Jernigan to 40 years on each count, with 20 years to serve without the possibility of parole in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections and 20 years suspended on probation. The sentences will run concurrently.

Jernigan also was ordered to pay a $1,000 assessment to the Victims of Human Trafficking and Commercial Sexual Exploitation Fund and $1,000 to the Mississippi Children’s Trust Fund. He must register as a sex offender.

According to the Attorney General’s Office, the investigation began after concerned parents reported that children were being solicited online for sexually explicit photos and videos.

The case was investigated and prosecuted by the Attorney General’s Office with assistance from the Smith County Sheriff’s Office, Raleigh Police Department, Faribault County Sheriff’s Office and District Attorney Chris Hennis’ Office.

Fitch encouraged parents to maintain open communication with children about online activity and internet safety. The Attorney General’s Office said anyone with information about online child exploitation should contact the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children CyberTipline at 1-800-843-5678 or report tips online.

item.title: Former Jones County road foreman, contractor plead guilty in embezzlement case - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JONES COUNTY – A former Jones County road foreman and a contractor have pleaded guilty in connection with a scheme to embezzle county-owned culverts, State Auditor Shad White announced.

According to the State Auditor’s Office, Richard Creel pleaded guilty to one count of embezzlement, and Tommie Landrum pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit and one count of accessory before the fact.

White’s office said Creel and Landrum were involved in a scheme to embezzle county-owned culverts and transport the property to a predetermined location provided by Landrum.

“The dedicated team at the State Auditor’s office has a zero-tolerance policy for fraud and we will continue to work with prosecutors to get record results for taxpayers,” White said.

Both men were prosecuted in Jones County Circuit Court.

Creel was sentenced to five years of post-release supervision and was ordered to pay $4,925.24 in restitution and $2,927.50 in fines.

Landrum was sentenced to five years, with two years suspended after completion of three years of non-adjudicated probation. He was also ordered to pay $2,462.62 in restitution and $2,927.50 in fines.

Suspected fraud can be reported to the Auditor’s Office by clicking the red button on the office’s website or by calling 1-800-321-1275 during normal business hours.

COLLINSVILLE – Two small female dogs recently taken in by East Mississippi Animal Rescue will soon be available for adoption after they receive veterinary care.

The dogs, Edie and Blair, are believed to be possible Yorkie-Chihuahua mixes. Edie has short hair, while Blair has long hair, according to the rescue.

East Mississippi Animal Rescue said the dogs were surrendered by a breeder from another county to a different rescue before East Mississippi Animal Rescue was able to help.

The rescue is asking for donations to help cover the cost of their veterinary care at Collinsville Vet. Officials said the vetting is expected to cost around $200 per dog, possibly more. The rescue is also asking for prayers that both dogs test negative for heartworms.

Donations may be made directly to Collinsville Vet by calling 601-626-7738. The rescue also accepts PayPal donations through its website at EastMSAnimalRescue.com.

Once the dogs have been vetted and cleared, they will be available for adoption. East Mississippi Animal Rescue said the dogs just arrived and appear to be friendly, though the rescue is still learning more about them.

Those interested in adopting are encouraged to submit a pre-application soon. The adoption fee is $250.

item.title: CARA to host 17th annual Dog Days of Summer fundraiser - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Community Animal Rescue & Adoption, known as CARA, will host its 17th annual Dog Days of Summer fundraiser on Saturday, June 6, at LeFleur’s Bluff State Park.

The event will be held from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. at 3315 Lakeland Terrace in Jackson. All proceeds will go directly to the care of CARA’s shelter animals.

Organizers said the family-friendly event will include a Children’s Village with attractions such as Snake Man Joe and his animal friends, a large bounce house from Ace Inflatables, cosplay characters from Mississippi Metahumans, face painting, games, bubbles, crafts and freebies. Blue Bell Creameries will also provide free ice cream.

Other activities will include agility demonstrations, K-9 demonstrations, a blessing of the animals ceremony, a silent auction, microchipping, adoptable CARA dogs, arts and crafts vendors, music, a pet parade and pet contests.

Food and drinks will also be available, including lunches by Outback Steakhouse, pizza from Lost Pizza Co., Raising Cane’s iced tea and lemonade, and Blue Bell ice cream.

Admission to the Children’s Village is $5 for all-day access. General admission is a monetary donation or a donation of dry or canned dog food, with Purina brands preferred.

Attendees are invited to bring the entire family, including pets. Pets should be kept on a secure leash.

CARA said Dog Days of Summer is its biggest fundraiser of the year and helps support the animals in its care. More information is available on their website.

You won’t want to miss this incredible event!

Go have fun with your family and support this incredible rescue!

item.title: Rare, fully preserved cast iron casket recovered from Asylum Hill excavation - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
By Alexandria Galtney University of Mississippi Medical Center

JACKSON – Archaeologists excavating remains from the site of the Asylum Hill Cemetery on the University of Mississippi Medical Center campus have unearthed a rare, fully preserved cast iron casket dating back to the late 1800s.

The rusted casket, which weighed nearly 200 pounds and was sealed with 24 heavily corroded bolts, was discovered in March by a six-member excavation team near the ridge of the cemetery. Researchers say the find is unlike anything uncovered since the excavation project began.

Dr. Jennifer Mack, lead bioarcheologist, said cast iron caskets were uncommon in institutional cemeteries because of their cost.

“We have seen in the patient records where someone has said, well I can’t get my loved one, but we are going to wire this much money for the purchase of a casket,” said Mack. “It wasn’t uncommon for people to send the money for a burial here, but the cast iron casket is just a particularly pricey example of that.”

According to Mack, it is possible the individual’s family purchased the casket with plans to reclaim their loved one, but those plans may have changed.

Historical records indicate that a cast iron casket in 1865 cost approximately $44.11 wholesale, including shipping and a protective shipping box. In contrast, a plain wooden coffin during the same period costs about $2.50.

Dr. Ralph Didlake, director of the Asylum Hill project and a skilled carpenter, created a reconstruction of what a simple wooden coffin from that era would have looked like for those buried in the cemetery. He noted that burial practices and transportation methods were markedly different at the time and emphasized that the stories of those interred at the site are of significant historical interest.

“It’s less about the individual coffin than it is about the individual story of the Asylum cemetery and the fact that it is very deep,” said Didlake. “Everyone is an individual and every story has meaning because it reflects the time and it reflects us. These people all have a name and an experience and relationships and the stories, and how we preserve them reflects on us.”

Mack said it took the team more than two hours to open the casket using a drill. Once opened, researchers discovered cracks in the lid and sides and a damaged glass viewing pane beneath its metal cover. The damage likely accelerated the deterioration of the remains inside.

Researchers believe the individual was a woman of European ancestry between the ages of 30 and 55 at the time of her death. Mack estimated the woman stood between 4 feet, 9 inches and just over 5 feet tall.

The only personal item recovered from the casket was a brass ring with a red glass center “gem.” Researchers also found the woman had lost all of her teeth before her death, making identification more difficult.

Mack said the excavation crew worked closely with UMMC’s Department of Environmental Health and Safety, the biological safety officer, the chemical safety officer, and Employee Occupational Health Services to ensure the safety of both the team and the public throughout the recovery process.

The Department of Advanced Biomedical Education provided expertise, protective equipment, and secure storage for the remains until testing confirmed there was no biohazard risk. The Center for Comparative Research remained on standby to provide additional analysis space if needed, while the Department of Biomedical Materials Science is currently analyzing samples to determine whether embalming chemicals are present.

According to biological safety officer Anthony Walters, the opening of the cast iron casket was a carefully coordinated effort. While there was initial hesitancy due to concerns about its contents, multiple safety procedures were in place prior to opening. Walters noted that despite those concerns, there was also a sense of anticipation, and the team worked quickly to ensure preservation efforts were maintained.

“From a biological safety standpoint, we were able to learn a lot because it was a unique situation, so we were able to see this is what we are capable of and maybe these are some areas we can adjust a little bit,” said Walters. “I think this gives us a much broader view of the historical health of Mississippi and a better understanding of what the Asylum did and who was here because there are a lot of misconceptions.”

Didlake, Walters and Mack are hoping this new discovery will help change the narrative of Mississippi and also shape the state’s future.

“We have a, in a very tangible way, inherited these patients, and we will take care of them in a very ethical, respectable way,” said Didlake. “It cuts across our education mission; we have created opportunities for students to come and others to come and learn about how this type of work is done. We will certainly leverage every opportunity to do appropriate research through the excavation and learn about the remains, but even overarching is that the project will provide and allow us to repurpose land for the campus for our future patients.”

While excavation crews have uncovered remains from wooden caskets throughout the project, this marks the first cast iron casket recovered from the site.

The team is awaiting results of X-ray imaging on the remains in hopes of learning more about the woman’s possible cause of death. Researchers estimate between 5,000 and 7,000 individuals are buried within the cemetery’s 12-and-a-half-acre site. Mack said the estimate is based on a 1948 engineering plan and calculations of burial density across the property. At least 1,065 bodies have been exhumed.

To support the ongoing excavation efforts, the Mississippi Legislature appropriated more than $3.68 million to the Asylum Hill Project.

item.title: Motorcyclist accused of leading Capitol Police on 140 mph chase - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – A man was arrested after Capitol Police said he led officers on a high-speed chase from Jackson to Crystal Springs early Wednesday morning.

Capitol Police officers attempted to stop a motorcycle traveling at a high rate of speed on Ridgewood Road around 5:39 a.m., according to PIO, Bailey C. Martin.

Authorities said the motorcycle fled from officers, leading them through multiple roads and onto Interstate 55 South at speeds exceeding 140 mph.

The pursuit continued into Crystal Springs, where the driver was identified as Kyle King, 33. King was taken into custody on Ruby Road with assistance from the Copiah County Sheriff’s Office.

King is charged with felony fleeing and possession of paraphernalia involving methamphetamine. Authorities said he also had warrants from other surrounding jurisdictions.

No additional information was immediately released.

item.title: Two men dead after separate Hinds County ATV, side-by-side crashes - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
HINDS COUNTY – Two men died after separate crashes involving off-road vehicles in Hinds County, according to Hinds County Coroner Jeramiah Howard.

The first crash happened Saturday, May 16, in the 3600 block of McFarland Road in Raymond.

Authorities said Timothy Bright, 59, of Jackson, was a passenger in a side-by-side that left the roadway and overturned. Bright died at the scene.

A second crash happened May 9 in the 1600 block of South Norrell Road in Bolton.

Authorities said Andy Sanders, 56, of Bolton, was driving an ATV that left the roadway and struck a tree. Sanders died from his injuries at a local hospital on Friday, May 15.

item.title: Starkville Man Charged After Reported Assault With Bat - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
STARKVILLE – A Starkville man has been charged after police said he entered a home, struck a woman with a bat and attempted to strangle her.

The Starkville Police Department said officers responded Sunday, May 17, around 11 a.m. to a report of an assault that had occurred earlier that day at a residence on Peoples Street.

Police said the victim was treated at Baptist Memorial Hospital-Oktibbeha County and later released.

Blair Bell, 35, of Starkville, was charged with domestic violence-aggravated assault and residential burglary. Police said Bell turned himself in Monday morning.

The incident remains under investigation.

According to the National Coalition Against Domestic Violence, 1 in 4 women and 1 in 7 men in the United States have experienced severe physical violence by an intimate partner during their lifetime.

Anyone with information about the incident or other criminal activity is asked to contact the Starkville Police Department at 662-323-4131, Golden Triangle Crime Stoppers at 800-530-7151, or submit an anonymous tip through the department’s website. Crime Stoppers may offer a cash reward.

item.title: Southern Pines to host free feline vaccination clinic in Hattiesburg - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
HATTIESBURG — Southern Pines Animal Shelter will host a free feline vaccination clinic on Friday, May 22, at its Healthy Pet Clinic in downtown Hattiesburg.

The event will take place from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Southern Pines Healthy Pet Clinic, located at 1304 Hardy St., next to Great Southern Bank.

The clinic will provide two free vaccines for cats, including the HCP feline vaccine, which protects against panleukopenia and is being provided through Petco Love, as well as rabies vaccines required under Mississippi law.

To qualify, cats must be at least 6 weeks old, healthy and comfortable being handled. All cats must be brought in secure carriers.

Walk-ins will be accepted, but appointments are encouraged. Pet owners can schedule appointments through the clinic’s website at Southern Pines Healthy Pet Clinic by selecting “Feline Vaccine Event.”

The clinic will also offer eligible cats the opportunity to participate in a research study examining the safety of a new vaccine. Cats enrolled in the 21-day study will receive a free wellness package upon completion. Additional information is available by emailing [email protected] .

According to Southern Pines, the Healthy Pet Clinic opened in 2009 and has altered more than 84,000 pets as part of efforts to address pet overpopulation in the Pine Belt. The clinic provides low-cost veterinary services and surgeries for area pets and is open Monday through Saturday.

For more information, call 601-544-5678.

item.title: Southaven police searching for hit-and-run driver after child seriously injured on minibike - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
SOUTHAVEN — Police are searching for the driver of a black Mercedes believed to have struck a 9-year-old child riding a minibike Saturday afternoon before leaving the scene.

According to the Southaven Police Department, the crash happened around 2:57 p.m. May 16 in the area of Chesterfield Drive and Farmington North.

Investigators said the child was riding a small minibike when the vehicle struck the minibike and continued south on Chesterfield Drive without stopping.

Police described the vehicle as a black Mercedes, possibly an S550 model, with a black Mississippi tag and tinted windows. Authorities said the vehicle should have damage to the front driver’s side bumper area.

The child was transported to Le Bonheur Children’s Hospital with serious injuries. Police said the child was last reported in stable condition.

Anyone with information about the vehicle or its owner is asked to contact the Southaven Police Department at 662-393-8652 or email [email protected] .

item.title: SCRMC recognizes three employees with 50 years of faithful service - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
The year was 1975. The Vietnam War was coming to a close, Microsoft had just been founded and Bruce Springsteen was topping the charts. South Central Regional Medical Center, which was called Jones County Community Hospital at the time, had just entered its third decade of faithfully serving the Pine Belt, and three young women joined the staff: Judy Hicks, Nell Warren and Jodie Mancil. Today, a half-century later, South Central Regional Medical Center wants to pause and celebrate the impact they have made on the organization.

Judy Hicks

Judy is a Laurel native who spent most of her adolescence living in Germany, France, Belgium and in various states across the eastern seaboard. Her father was in the Army, and moving was part of the job. When her father retired, the whole family moved back to Laurel, and Judy, who was 21 at the time, began working in admissions at Jones County Community Hospital in July 1975.

“I didn’t know what insurance was or what a policy was,” Judy said. “I was working from noon until 9 p.m., and I remember telling my dad, ‘I don’t like it. I want to quit.’ Then he said, ‘you have not been there long enough. Give it six months.’”

Judy did as her father suggested and to her surprise, she fell in love with the challenge of her work, devoting 50 years of her professional career to advocating for patients and navigating evolving regulations.

After two years of working in admissions, Judy was transferred to working in the insurance department. Judy recalls the adjustment to working in insurance as having been difficult.

Judy was later promoted to a supervisory role and eventually became Director of Patient Accounts. She served in this role until 2019 and now is in the process of training others to fill her shoes.

Judy’s devotion to her work is admirable, showing that persistence and gumption go a long way in creating a lasting career.

Nell Warren Nell is a Paulding native who graduated from South Side High School in Heidelberg.

She first began working in dietary at Jones County Community Hospital as a helper, where she prepped tube feeds for patients, worked in the dish room and worked in the food line.

“I have done pretty much everything except cook, I haven’t done any of that,” Nell said.

Today, Nell can be found in the physicians’ lounge at South Central Regional Medical Center, where she ensures that physicians are well taken care of nutritionally, while always offering a smile or words of encouragement.

“I love people,” Nell said. “I love being around people. I like to hug.”

Nell’s presence is a reminder that care is not only clinical, it is human.

Jodie Mancil

Jodie Mancil was born in Texas but lived abroad for thirteen years. Her father worked in the oil business and the company he worked for relocated her family to Sicily, Italy, and Tripoli, Libya. She even attended boarding school in Switzerland for a brief period, while her parents worked in Mozambique, Africa.

“My father asked to be transferred so that the family could be a unit again before my sister and I were grown and married; and they moved him from Africa to Soso, Mississippi,” Jodie said.

Jodie lived in the area and earned a bachelor’s degree in medical technology from the University of Southern Mississippi. She began working at Jones County Community Hospital in July 1975 as a medical technologist.

Throughout the years, she has become an integral member of the lab team. She has served as the blood bank supervisor for almost ten years, and in this role, she teaches students who come into the lab as part of their training.

“It is my calling from the Lord to teach, and I enjoy teaching,” Jodie said. “I enjoy helping others. If you look at it as a ministry, it is not a job. Some days are harder than others, but in the end the Lord has you here for a reason. I try to tell my students to bloom where they are planted, and I am planted here.”

Judy, Nell and Jodie’s stories teach us many lessons, but one lesson stands out among the rest — it is that perspective shapes purpose. For Judy, work brought fulfillment. For Nell, it brought connection. For Jodie, it became a mission field. When work is rooted in meaning, it becomes more than a job, it becomes a life calling.

item.title: Rienzi man accused of taking $12,300 for home repairs, abandoning project - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
PRENTISS COUNTY – A Rienzi man has been arrested in connection with an ongoing home repair fraud investigation in Prentiss County.

The Prentiss County Sheriff’s Department said Jacob Stewart, 32, was arrested after two people reported that he accepted $12,300 for repair work at their home but only performed minimal labor before abandoning the project.

Deputy Peeks took the complaint April 22, and the case was assigned to Investigator Aaron Stolz.

Investigators collected financial records, a contract, photographs of the property and statements from the complainants. An affidavit was submitted to Justice Court for review.

Justice Court Judge Craig Bishop issued a warrant for Stewart’s arrest. On May 13, investigators Torie Jumper and Aaron Stolz made contact with Stewart and took him into custody.

Stewart appeared before Bishop on May 14 for his initial appearance. His bond was set at $25,000 professional bond.

item.title: Retired Southaven police K-9 dies after years of service - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
SOUTHAVEN – The Southaven Police Department is mourning the loss of a retired police service dog.

The department said Ziggy, an 11-year-old Belgian Malinois, died Saturday, May 16, while with his former handler and family.

Ziggy served the Southaven Police Department as a patrol and explosive detection K-9 from 2018 to 2024. Before joining the department, he served as a military working dog with the Army Ranger Battalion.

Police said Ziggy was known for his speed, strength and work apprehending numerous suspects. He also assisted surrounding agencies with explosive sweeps in DeSoto County when needed.

One of Ziggy’s most notable cases happened Aug. 7, 2020, when police said he helped track three armed suspects who fled on foot from a stolen vehicle. The suspects also were accused in several auto burglaries at a Southaven apartment complex. Within an hour, Ziggy tracked all three suspects and apprehended two of them. The third suspect surrendered without incident.

After retiring, Ziggy spent the rest of his life at home with his former handler and family.

The Southaven Police Department said Ziggy was loved by many in the department and left a lasting impact.

item.title: Renowned "Bulletproof Mind" author Lt. Col. Dave Grossman to headline Mississippi resilience conference - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
RANKIN COUNTY — Lt. Col. Dave Grossman, the retired Army officer and author widely known for his work on the psychology of combat and law enforcement performance, is set to headline a three-day conference aimed at police officer wellness next month in Flowood.

The 2026 Shield Summit, hosted by the Mississippi National Guard’s Regional Counterdrug Training Academy, is scheduled for June 9-11 at the Northwest Rankin Middle School Performance Arts Building at 5805 Highway 25.

Grossman will deliver his signature “Bulletproof Mind” presentation, an eight-hour session focused on preparing officers to manage their response to high-stress and violent encounters. The conference, billed under the acronym P.O.L.I.C.E. — Police Officer Life Issues and Career Endurance — is framed around officer resilience, wellness and career longevity.

Programming across the three days is structured around what organizers call a “Sheepdog” framework, a nod to the concept Sheep, Wolves, and Sheepdogs in Grossman’s “On Combat,” with topics including mental fortitude, PTSD and stress management, suicide prevention, career and family balance, and performance optimization.

The event is the second annual resilience conference put on by the RCTA. Check back here for a list of speakers Monday afternoon.

item.title: Orientation welcomes incoming Bulldogs, celebrates century with gallery exhibit - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
STARKVILLE — Since 1926, Mississippi State’s Orientation sessions have offered new Bulldogs a warm welcome. As MSU Orientation marks 100 years, an exhibit highlighting the program’s history is opening in the Colvard Student Union Art Gallery.

“It’s a special year to be able to look back over the past century. While times have changed, the main goals have remained constant—welcoming students, easing their anxieties as they enroll, assisting with their class schedules and providing helpful information,” said Director of Orientation and Events Jake Hartfield.

The “100 Years of Orientation at Mississippi State” exhibit, located on the Union’s second floor, is open throughout the summer. A come-and-go reception will be held May 29, 3:30-5 p.m., and Hartfield encouraged alumni, current and former administrators and everyone affiliated with the Orientation program, past or present, to mark the occasion and interact with current Orientation Leaders.

Students and their guests attending MSU Orientation sessions this summer also can view the exhibit, which includes photographs, pamphlets and even clothing items from past years. Orientation Leaders, or OLs as they are sometimes known, play a major role in hosting new students and their families, answering questions and shepherding students into university life.

Hartfield, who also served as an OL during his own student days at MSU, said the group has been a key part of setting the tone for Southern hospitality to newcomers since it formed in 1979.

“Each Orientation session is an all-hands-on-deck event. From our Orientation Leaders to our staff members, administrators and advisors, we want to roll out the maroon carpet for our new students, no matter if it’s the first or the last session. We want to ensure that everybody’s getting the same exciting, high-energy experience,” Hartfield said.

With over 5,000 incoming students attending summer Orientation, the program hosts more than 10,000 total, including parents and other guests, across approximately 15 sessions. MSU President Mark E. Keenum has attended Orientation throughout his tenure, and each event includes a variety of university speakers, panels, ice cream socials and the iconic MSU Orientation original skit, which pays homage each year to a distinctive part of student life.

“It takes a lot of energy and a servant’s heart to provide the best experience possible. We want to make sure our new students have the resources they need to feel they’re in good hands, prepared and that they made the right choice in choosing Mississippi State,” Hartfield said.

To further mark the 100-year milestone, university leaders are planning a fall tailgate for current and former Orientation Leaders, administrators and staff. The MSU Foundation also has an MSU Orientation Leaders Excellence Fund available at www.dda.msstate.edu/give-now?f=313024 .

Incoming students can confirm their MSU enrollment by signing up for Orientation at www.orientation.msstate.edu .

item.title: Mississippi mourns Buddy Cooper, beloved bus driver, Santa Claus - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
FLORENCE — Alex Cooper, a longtime Florence school bus driver and beloved local Santa Claus known to generations of families across Rankin County and the state, has died after suffering critical injuries in a school bus crash earlier this month.

Cooper, known affectionately throughout the community as “Buddy,” died Saturday, May 16, according to a Facebook post from his son, Gabe Cooper.

“My dad went home to be with Jesus today,” Gabe Cooper wrote. “I want to deeply thank the support system the family has had throughout this ordeal.”

The crash happened May 11 on Highway 49 near Eagle Post Road in Florence when an 18-wheeler struck a Rankin County school bus head-on, according to authorities. Cooper was driving the bus at the time. Family members said the brakes on the 18-wheeler went out.

Officials said there were no students on the bus during the crash.

Cooper, 79, suffered catastrophic injuries and was rushed to the hospital in critical condition. Family members later said he was paralyzed from the neck down and battling internal injuries following the wreck.

In a fundraising campaign created after the crash, Gabe Cooper described his father as a man who spent decades serving the community both behind the wheel of a school bus and as a familiar face during the Christmas season.

“For years, he has brought joy to children and families as Santa Claus during the Christmas season,” the fundraiser said. “Whether driving a school bus, lending a helping hand, or making children smile in a Santa suit, he has spent his life serving others and loving this community well.”

In the days following the crash, social media filled with tributes from former students, parents and community members sharing memories of Cooper’s kindness and generosity.

Beyond driving a school bus, Cooper became widely known across Mississippi for portraying Santa Claus at community events, shopping malls, parades, and official holiday celebrations. In a previous interview with Darkhorse Press during a Christmas event, Cooper reflected on one of his proudest moments as Santa.

“The crowning achievement of my term as Santa is being Santa for the Governor, the First Lady, and you, the people of Mississippi,” Cooper said.

The Florence Police Department investigated the crash.

Gabe Cooper said the family plans to announce details for a celebration of life at a later time. In lieu of flowers, the family requested donations be made to The Little Lighthouse.

Editor’s note: Buddy Cooper was a friend and a dear brother in Christ. Our deepest condolences to his family. The light he brought to our lives and especially our Christmases will never go out.

item.title: Operation Hope launched to locate Mississippi's missing foster children, 13 recovered - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced the launch of Operation Hope on Monday, a new multi-agency initiative aimed at locating missing foster children, with authorities saying 13 children were found and brought to safety during the operation.

Fitch joined U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Administration for Children and Families Assistant Secretary Alex J. Adams, HHS Inspector General T. March Bell and Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services Commissioner Andrea Sanders to announce the program.

Officials said the operation combined law enforcement, child welfare agencies and support services in an effort to locate vulnerable children in foster care before they could be exploited or harmed.

“We are proud to have helped kick off this program here in Mississippi,” Fitch said. “Over the past several weeks of planning and in the execution of the operation last week, it was always our intention not only to locate vulnerable Mississippi youth but also to create a model that can be used in other states.”

Fitch said the effort was designed to show children “that they matter, and that they deserve hope.”

Adams said the operation recovered 87% of the missing foster youth identified during the initiative in less than 48 hours.

“To continue serving the best interests of children, Operation Hope will be replicated in other states, and we will leave no stone unturned when searching for these kids,” Adams said.

Bell, the HHS inspector general, said missing foster children require “a rapid, multi-faceted law enforcement response” and called the Mississippi effort a model for other states.

Sanders, commissioner of the Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services, said the operation focused on ensuring vulnerable children knew “someone was looking for them.”

“Every child located through this operation represents a young person who matters deeply and deserves safety, support, and hope for the future,” Sanders said.

Officials said children located during the operation were offered support services in addition to being recovered safely.

According to the announcement, the federal government first launched a similar initiative known as Project Hope in Kansas and Missouri, where officials said 42 missing children were located.

item.title: Mississippi awarding more than $23 million for local infrastructure projects statewide - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Gov. Tate Reeves’ office announced Monday that more than $23 million in federal Community Development Block Grant funding will be distributed to cities and counties across Mississippi for infrastructure and public facilities projects.

The $23,035,043.12 in funding, administered through the Mississippi Development Authority, will support projects including sewer and water system improvements, stormwater drainage upgrades, road work, ADA improvements and public building renovations.

The federally authorized Community Development Block Grant program is designed to help communities improve essential services, address blight and respond to urgent public needs. Projects must meet at least one national objective, including benefiting low- and moderate-income residents or addressing threats to public health and safety.

Other communities receiving funding include Brookhaven, Belzoni, Terry, Union, Taylorsville, Pelahatchie, Columbia, Ellisville, Charleston and Rosedale.

item.title: MISSING IN MISSISSIPPI: Deborah Faye Owens, Forrest County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
HATTIESBURG — It’s been more than 42 years since Deborah Faye Owens allegedly stepped out of her husband’s vehicle into nowhere on a New Year’s morning.

Investigators still have no answers about what happened to the 27-year-old woman after she and her husband left a New Year’s Eve celebration in the early hours of Jan. 1, 1984.

According to the Hattiesburg Police Department, Owens was last seen after attending the party with her husband. Authorities said the couple allegedly got into an argument while driving home, and her husband told investigators that Owens asked to be let out of the vehicle.

He told police he pulled over and let her out, then drove away. Owens has not been seen or heard from since.

Owens was a white female, and at the time of her disappearance, she was 27 years old.

A 1985 report in The Clarion-Ledger quoted Hattiesburg Detective Bob Hopkins as saying that Owens’ disappearance was unusual because she had always remained in contact with family or friends in the past.

“It’s not the first time she’s done something like this, but it’s the first time she hasn’t contacted anyone,” Hopkins told the newspaper.

In the months after Owens vanished, local newspapers published classified legal notices in April 1984 seeking a divorce from “Deborah Faye Owens, whose last known address was Hattiesburg, Mississippi but whose present residence and address is unknown,” citing cruel and unusual treatment.

Little additional information about the case was publicly released in the years that followed. Owens’ name appeared briefly in a 1987 Clarion-Ledger story about unresolved missing persons cases in Mississippi, but no major developments have ever been announced.

Today, Owens’ disappearance remains unsolved.

Anyone with information about Deborah Faye Owens or her disappearance is asked to contact the Hattiesburg Police Department at (601) 545-4971.

GULFPORT- A Gulfport man was arrested Sunday after police said he fled from officers in a vehicle connected to a recent burglary investigation.

The Gulfport Police Department said Roy Rodney Robinson, 58, of Gulfport, was arrested May 17 and charged with one count of felony fleeing and one count of burglary of a vehicle.

Police said officers saw a vehicle connected to a recent vehicle burglary around 6:17 p.m. in the area of 34th Street near 13th Avenue. When officers tried to stop the vehicle, Robinson accelerated and fled, according to police.

Investigators said Robinson drove at a high rate of speed, disregarded multiple traffic control devices and drove recklessly.

Police said Robinson later approached the area of 34th Street near Jody Nelson Drive, where an officer was positioned off the roadway preparing to deploy spike strips. Robinson allegedly braked and steered the Lexus toward the officer before hitting a curb. Police said he then put the vehicle in reverse and accelerated, striking the front end of a patrol vehicle.

Robinson and a passenger were taken into custody and transported to the Gulfport Police Department. Police said both were found to have active felony warrants out of Missouri.

Robinson was taken to the Harrison County Adult Detention Center, where he was being held on a $175,000 bond. The passenger was held without bond pending extradition.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Gulfport Police Department at 228-868-5959 or Mississippi Coast Crime Stoppers at 877-787-5898.

item.title: Greenville man charged after domestic shooting investigation - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
GREENVILLE – A man was arrested after Greenville police investigated a domestic-related shooting early Saturday morning.

The Greenville Police Department said officers responded around 12:40 a.m. May 16 to the 1400 block of Highway 1 South for a reported shooting connected to a domestic dispute.

While officers were on the way, they were told the suspect had returned to the scene in a black Chevrolet Impala. Officers found the vehicle and detained four people without incident, police said.

During the investigation, officers recovered multiple firearms from inside the vehicle, including handguns and a rifle. The firearms were secured as evidence.

Police said the incident began near the Express Inn on U.S. 82 East after an altercation between the suspect and the victim. Investigators said that after a vehicle collision, the suspect allegedly followed the victim and fired multiple rounds into her vehicle, striking it at least once.

Based on witness statements, physical evidence and statements obtained during the investigation, Dannarius Hartman was arrested and charged with domestic aggravated assault.

No injuries were reported.

Police said the investigation remains active, and additional charges or arrests are possible.

item.title: Four women arrested after drug search within 1,000 feet of churches in Greenville - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
GREENVILLE – Four women were arrested Friday after Greenville police executed a search warrant as part of an ongoing narcotics investigation.

The Greenville Police Department said members of its Special Response Team and Special Operations Unit executed the court-authorized search warrant around 8:37 a.m. May 15 at a residence on Wallstreet Lane.

Police said officers announced their presence but did not receive a response before entering the home. Four adult women inside the residence were safely detained while officers secured the home and conducted a search.

During the search, investigators said they recovered suspected methamphetamine, drug paraphernalia, syringes, digital scales, packaging materials and other items commonly associated with illegal narcotics activity.

Tia Spencer was charged with possession of drug paraphernalia.

Marsha Reid, Tammie Smith and Amanda Manning were each charged with enhanced possession of methamphetamine and possession of drug paraphernalia.

Investigators said the residence was within 1,000 feet of active churches, resulting in enhanced charges under Mississippi narcotics laws.

All four were taken to the Greenville Police Department for processing.

Police said the investigation remains active, and additional charges or arrests may follow.

Anyone with information about illegal drug activity is asked to contact the Greenville Police Department or local Crime Stoppers.
